A graph's structure is only half of most analyses. The other half is the data attached to its nodes
and edges: the ages of people in a social network, the capacities of pipes in a supply network, the
scores computed by an algorithm. EdgeCase stores this data as named attributes on each node and
edge, and offers three ways to work with it: as dictionaries keyed by ID, as Polars DataFrames, and
through selections. This page covers the first two; [Selections](08-selections.qmd) covers the
third.

| Task | Methods |
|---|---|
| Read everything as a table | [`get_node_df()`](../reference/Graph.get_node_df.qmd), [`get_edge_df()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_df.qmd) |
| Read one attribute | [`get_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.get_node_attrs.qmd), [`get_edge_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_attrs.qmd), [`get_edge_attrs_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_attrs_by_id.qmd) |
| Read one node or edge | [`get_node()`](../reference/Graph.get_node.qmd), [`get_edge()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge.qmd) |
| Write one attribute | [`set_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.set_node_attrs.qmd), [`set_edge_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.set_edge_attrs.qmd) |
| Map values to visual properties | [`rescale_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.rescale_node_attrs.qmd), [`colorize_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.colorize_node_attrs.qmd) |

## The node and edge tables

[`get_node_df()`](../reference/Graph.get_node_df.qmd) returns one row per node as a Polars
DataFrame. Its layout is always the same, so code that reads it never has to guess:

- the `id`, `label`, and `type` columns come first,
- the node's attributes follow, in alphabetical order, and
- a `degree` column, computed on the spot, comes last.

The rows are sorted by ID. The Florentine families dataset makes a good running example:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

florentine = ec.florentine_families()
florentine.get_node_df().head(5)
```

[`get_edge_df()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_df.qmd) is the edge counterpart. Its first columns
are `id`, `source`, `target`, and `rel`, followed by `weight` when any edge has one, and then the
other edge attributes in alphabetical order:

```{python}
florentine.get_edge_df().head(5)
```

Both tables are fresh copies. Changing a DataFrame never changes the graph, so filter, sort, and
reshape them freely; writing results back into the graph is a separate step, shown below.

A Polars column holds values of one data type, so when an attribute's values differ in type from
node to node, the table reconciles them: integers beside floats become floats, and a single value
beside lists becomes a one-item list. Other mixtures, such as strings beside numbers, give a column
of Python objects that holds the values unchanged. Storing each attribute with one consistent type
keeps the tables easy to work with.

## Reading attributes

To read a single attribute, [`get_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.get_node_attrs.qmd) is lighter
than building a whole table. It returns a dictionary from node ID to value, and leaves out the nodes
that don't have the attribute. Its `nodes=` argument narrows the result to some nodes:

```{python}
karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.get_node_attrs("role", nodes=[1, 2, 34])
```

The edge equivalent, [`get_edge_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_attrs.qmd), returns a
dictionary keyed by edge ID. Its `sources=` and `targets=` arguments keep only the edges that leave
or enter particular nodes, and `"weight"` reads the edge weights:

```{python}
les_mis = ec.les_miserables()
les_mis.get_edge_attrs("weight", sources=["Valjean"])
```

In an undirected graph, `sources=` and `targets=` match an edge in either orientation, so this
returns every edge that touches Valjean, whichever way round it was recorded. Valjean has 36 of
them. When the edge IDs are already known, from `find_edge_ids()` or a selection,
[`get_edge_attrs_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_attrs_by_id.qmd) reads them directly.

For everything about a single node or edge, `get_node()` and `get_edge()` return objects with the
ID, the label or endpoints, and a dictionary of all attributes, as described in
[The graph model](03-graph-model.qmd#types-and-attributes).

## Writing attributes

[`set_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.set_node_attrs.qmd) writes one attribute, creating it if it
doesn't exist and overwriting it if it does. Its `values=` argument takes one of three forms:

- **a single value**, written to every target node,
- **a list**, paired by position with the nodes in `nodes=`, or
- **a dictionary** from node IDs or labels to values, which updates only the nodes it names.

`nodes=` chooses the target nodes, and defaults to all of them. A single value is the way to tag a
group of nodes:

```{python}
florentine.set_node_attrs("faction", "Medici", nodes=["Medici", "Tornabuoni", "Ridolfi"])
florentine.get_node_attrs("faction")
```

A dictionary is the way to bring in data from outside the graph. Here are the families' net
worths in 1427, in thousands of lira, from the tax records that John Padgett gathered alongside the
marriage data:

```{python}
wealth = {
    "Acciaiuoli": 10, "Albizzi": 36, "Barbadori": 55, "Bischeri": 44, "Castellani": 20,
    "Ginori": 32, "Guadagni": 8, "Lamberteschi": 42, "Medici": 103, "Pazzi": 48,
    "Peruzzi": 49, "Ridolfi": 27, "Salviati": 10, "Strozzi": 146, "Tornabuoni": 48,
}
florentine.set_node_attrs("wealth", wealth).get_node_attrs("wealth", nodes=["Medici", "Strozzi"])
```

Since `set_node_attrs()` returns the graph, the call chains straight into a check of two of the new
values.

Lists are paired with `nodes=` by position. Always pass `nodes=` with a list, since without it the
list is paired with the nodes in the graph's internal order, which isn't necessarily the order in
which they were added.

### Setting edge attributes

[`set_edge_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.set_edge_attrs.qmd) accepts the same three forms of
`values=`, with dictionaries keyed by edge ID. The edges to update can be chosen in four ways:

| Argument | Chooses |
|---|---|
| `edge_ids=` | edges by ID |
| `edges=` | every edge between each `(source, target)` pair, including parallel edges |
| `sources=`, `targets=` | edges that leave or enter the given nodes (both, when combined) |
| none of these | every edge |

Two attribute names are special. Setting `"weight"` sets the edge's weight, the value that weighted
algorithms read, and setting `"rel"` sets its relationship type:

```{python}
florentine.set_edge_attrs("rel", "marriage")
florentine.set_edge_attrs("rel", "medici_marriage", sources=["Medici"])
florentine.get_edge_df().head(5)
```

The second call overwrote the `rel` of every edge touching the Medici, which in an undirected graph
includes edges in which they are listed as the target.

## Moving data between the graph and Polars

The node table and the dictionary form of `set_node_attrs()` make a natural round trip: read the
table, compute with Polars, and write the result back. Here a column is derived from two others,
then stored as a new attribute:

```{python}
florentine.betweenness_centrality()

table = florentine.get_node_df().with_columns(
    (pl.col("betweenness_centrality") / pl.col("wealth")).alias("brokerage_per_lira")
)
florentine.set_node_attrs("brokerage_per_lira", dict(zip(table["id"], table["brokerage_per_lira"])))

(
    florentine.get_node_df()
    .select("label", "wealth", "betweenness_centrality", "brokerage_per_lira")
    .sort("betweenness_centrality", descending=True)
    .head(5)
)
```

The Strozzi were by far the richest family, worth nearly half as much again as the Medici, yet the
Medici's position in the marriage network gave them twice the betweenness of anyone else. The
Guadagni, among the poorest families, were the second most important brokers, so they get by far
the most brokerage per lira. The same
pattern works for joining external data: read your data into a DataFrame, join it to the node table
on `label`, and write the new columns back with `dict(zip(...))`.

## Attributes written by algorithms

Most algorithms that compute one value per node or per edge follow the same convention:

- By default, they store their result as an attribute named after the method, such as
  `pagerank` or `betweenness_centrality`, and return the graph, so calls chain.
- `attr_name=` stores the result under a different name, which allows several runs with different
  settings to sit side by side.
- `return_dict=True` returns the result as a dictionary instead, and leaves the graph unchanged.

```{python}
karate.pagerank().pagerank(damping=0.5, attr_name="pagerank_d50")
karate.get_node_df().select("label", "pagerank", "pagerank_d50").head(3)
```

```{python}
scores = karate.pagerank(return_dict=True)
max(scores, key=scores.get)
```

The dictionary form suits code that consumes the scores directly, and it pairs with
`set_node_attrs()` when you want to store the result after all, or store a transformed version of
it. Algorithms that return a single number (such as `get_transitivity()`) or a structure (such as
`shortest_path()`) don't store anything.

The graph keeps a record of the computations whose results it stores, and lists them in its summary,
along with the attribute each one wrote:

```{python}
karate
```

## Types and relationship types

Node `type` and edge `rel` are ordinary attributes in most respects, and both can be set with
`set_node_attrs()` and `set_edge_attrs()`. They get special treatment in three places:

- they always have their own column in the node and edge tables, even when no node or edge has one;
- Cypher queries read them as node labels and relationship types, so `(p:person)-[:knows]->()`
  matches on them (see [Cypher queries](10-cypher.qmd)); and
- many methods accept them as filters, and generators set them through `type=` and `rel=`.

A node can have more than one type, given as a list, which the node table shows as a list column:

```{python}
roles = (
    ec.Graph()
    .add_node("Ruth", type=["person", "author"])
    .add_node("Sam", type="person")
)
roles.get_node_df()
```

Filtering the table by type is a job for Polars. With list types, test membership with
`list.contains()`:

```{python}
roles.get_node_df().filter(pl.col("type").list.contains("author"))
```

## Visual attributes

Two methods turn attribute values into visual properties and store them as new attributes, for use
by the interactive [graph widget](25-interactive.qmd) or any other renderer.
[`rescale_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.rescale_node_attrs.qmd) maps a numeric attribute onto a
range of sizes, and [`colorize_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.colorize_node_attrs.qmd) maps a
categorical attribute onto a color palette:

```{python}
(
    karate
    .cmty_louvain()
    .rescale_node_attrs("pagerank", range=[0.3, 1.0])
    .colorize_node_attrs("cmty_louvain", palette="Set2")
    .get_node_df()
    .select("label", "pagerank", "size", "cmty_louvain", "color")
    .head(4)
)
```

The static [`plot()`](22-plotting.qmd) method doesn't need these, since its `color_by=` and
`size_by=` arguments read the attributes directly; see [Aesthetics](24-aesthetics.qmd).

## Things to know

- **Attributes can't currently be removed.** Setting an attribute to `None` stores `None`, which
  shows as `null` in the tables but still appears in `get_node_attrs()`. To drop an attribute
  completely, rebuild the graph from its tables without that column.
- **Some column names are reserved.** In the node table, `id`, `label`, and `degree` always hold
  the node's ID, label, and degree. An attribute with one of those names (such as the `degree`
  that `degrees()` stores) is left out of the table, so read it with `get_node_attrs()`. Likewise,
  `id`, `source`, and `target` are reserved in the edge table.
- **Changes are logged.** Each `set_node_attrs()` and `set_edge_attrs()` call appears in the
  graph's [step log](26-step-log.qmd), which also records the attribute updates made by
  algorithms.
